mechanisms: Phone ownership is a visible marker of social standing, so a desire for social inclusion drives a preference for functionality and multimedia capability.
Airtime scarcity and privacy fears make direct questions about phone use unreliable, because adolescents hide their usage behind missed calls and narrow definitions of 'use'.
Strong aspirations for tertiary education create a willingness to pay for mobile services that are seen as tools for personal advancement.
Gendered household and public-space routines dictate when and where boys and girls are available, so mobile interactions must match their separate schedules and contexts.
objection_patterns: Will I have enough airtime to respond?
Will I understand the questions being asked?
Does this fit into my daily routine at home or in public?
confidence: Mixed-methods and survey data from South African adolescent samples; mechanisms are robust for the studied cohorts, but magnitudes and generalisability beyond these groups are unknown.
